test_title: RRB NTPC CBT-I Official Paper (Held On: 25 Jan 2021 Shift 2)
subject: general
question: Which of the following two regions are biodiversity hot-spots of India?

options.text: Simplipal National Park and Satkosia Tiger Reserve
Kaziranga National Park and Eastern Ghats
Krishna Wildlife Sanctuary and Kolleru Bird Sanctuary

solution:
The correct answer is __**Western Ghats and Eastern Himalayas**__

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Western Ghats** and the **Eastern Himalayas** are two of the most significant biodiversity hotspots in India.
 
• Biodiversity hotspots are regions with a high level of endemic species that are also under significant threat from humans.
 
• The **Western Ghats** are known for their rich biodiversity, including a large number of endemic flora and fauna.
 
• The **Eastern Himalayas** are also recognized for their unique biodiversity and are home to many rare and endangered species.
 
• Conservation efforts are critical in these regions to protect the diverse ecosystems and species they harbor.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• The concept of biodiversity hotspots was first introduced by Norman Myers in 1988.
 
• India is one of the 17 megadiverse countries in the world, hosting around 7-8% of all recorded species, including over 45,000 plant species and 91,000 species of animals.
 
• Efforts to protect these hotspots include the establishment of protected areas, wildlife sanctuaries, and national parks.
 
• Human activities such as deforestation, habitat destruction, and climate change pose significant threats to these regions.
 
• International cooperation and local community involvement are essential for the effective conservation of biodiversity hotspots.
